title: Next Greater Node In Linked List
description: Brute force to optimized: a forward scan per node versus a single monotonic decreasing stack pass over the linked list's values.

content.title: Next Greater Node In Linked List

blocks.text: You are given the head of a linked list with n nodes. For each node, find the value of the NEXT node that has a strictly LARGER value than the current node's value. Return an integer array answer, where answer[i] is that next larger value for the i-th node (0-indexed, in list order), or 0 if no such node exists.

blocks.caption: A monotonic decreasing stack of indices resolves every node's "next larger value" in a single linear pass over the list's values

blocks.text: This is the "next greater element" problem applied directly to a linked list's sequence of values: for each node, find the value of the closest LATER node whose value strictly exceeds it, defaulting to 0 if none exists.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Next Taller Person in a Line, One Time
blocks.text: Exactly like the classic "next taller person" question, except this time it is asked for EVERY single person in the line at once (not just a selected few), and instead of a default of "-1" for "nobody taller exists," the convention here is simply "0."

blocks.caption: The stack holds indices still waiting for a bigger value; a new bigger arrival resolves the answer for every smaller value currently waiting

blocks.text: Recognizing this as a direct application of the "next greater element" pattern (just on a linked list's sequence of values instead of a plain array) is the key step; a monotonic decreasing stack then resolves every node's answer in a single pass.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The linked list's SEQUENTIAL order is all that matters here; converting it into a plain array of values first turns this directly into the standard "next greater element" problem.

Observation 2: Walking through the values left to right, maintaining a stack of indices still WAITING to find a bigger value further along: whenever a new value arrives that is bigger than the value at the stack's top index, that new value IS the answer for the top (and possibly more indices below it too).

Observation 3: Repeatedly popping and resolving while the stack's top value is still smaller correctly handles a single new arrival resolving MULTIPLE waiting indices at once.

Observation 4: Indices remaining on the stack after the full scan never found a bigger value, so those default to 0, exactly as the problem specifies.
This is the classic monotonic decreasing stack technique for "next greater element," applied to a linked list's sequence of values after converting it to a plain array.
For each node's value, scan forward through every later value until the first one strictly greater is found.

items: Convert the linked list into a plain array of values.
For each index i, scan every index j > i in order; the first value found strictly greater than values[i] is the answer; if none is found, the answer defaults to 0.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Working with a plain array of values (rather than actual linked list node references) simplifies the algorithm, since only the sequential order and values matter.
The result array is initialized to all 0s by default, directly matching the problem's "0 if none exists" requirement.

blocks.text: Correctly finds each node's next larger value, since it directly scans exactly as the definition requires.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2) in the worst case (for example, a strictly decreasing sequence, where every scan reaches all the way to the end).
Space: O(n), for the array converted from the linked list.
Limitation: repeating a forward scan for every node is wasteful; a single monotonic stack pass resolves ALL nodes' answers simultaneously.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rescans forward for every node independently. Instead, walk through the values ONCE, maintaining a monotonic decreasing stack of indices still waiting for their next bigger value. Whenever a new value is bigger than the value at the stack's top index, pop and record that new value as the top's answer, repeating until the stack's top no longer qualifies.

Convert the linked list to an array of values. Initialize a result array of 0s. Walk through the values with a stack of indices: while the stack is non-empty and the value at its top index is smaller than the current value, pop and set that index's result to the current value. Push the current index.
Use a monotonic decreasing stack of indices to resolve every node's next larger value in a single linear pass.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The results are [7,0,5,5,0], matching the expected output.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each index is pushed and popped at most once.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case.

Each index pushed onto the stack represents "a value still waiting to find something bigger further ahead." The moment a bigger value arrives, it is guaranteed to be the FIRST (nearest) bigger value for every smaller value currently sitting on top of the stack, since anything even bigger would have already resolved them earlier. This is the exact same reasoning underlying Next Greater Element I, applied here directly to the linked list's own sequence of values.

items: Converting the linked list to a plain array first is a reasonable simplification, since only the values and their sequential order matter, not the actual node references.
The result array's default value of 0 directly matches the problem's specified default for "no next larger value exists."
The stack stores INDICES (not values), allowing direct updates to the correct position in the result array once resolved.

items: Trying to solve this by walking the actual linked list node pointers directly with a stack of NODE references, when converting to a plain array of values first is simpler and equally correct.
Using the wrong default value (-1 instead of 0), which this specific problem requires.
Forgetting to repeatedly pop (using a while loop, not a single if) when a new value resolves multiple waiting indices at once.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Next greater/larger VALUE" for every position in a sequence (array OR linked list) points directly to the monotonic decreasing stack technique.

items: Why is converting to an array a reasonable first step here, rather than working with the linked list directly? Because only the values and their sequential order matter for this specific algorithm; the linked list's pointer structure itself is not otherwise needed.

How would you solve this while walking the ACTUAL linked list, without ever converting to an array? Track indices alongside actual node references on the stack, resolving the result array the same way, just deriving indices as the list is walked rather than upfront.

How does this compare to Next Greater Element II (a circular variant)? That problem additionally requires wrapping around to the START of the array/list if nothing qualifies within the initial single pass, requiring either a doubled iteration or modular indexing.
A direct application of the "next greater element" monotonic stack pattern from Next Greater Element I, relocated onto a linked list's sequence of values.

blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (monotonic decreasing stack): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Monotonic decreasing stack for "next greater element"
Core Idea: Convert the linked list to a plain array of values; a single monotonic decreasing stack pass resolves every node's next larger value simultaneously
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: This is exactly the Next Greater Element I pattern, just relocated onto a linked list's values, with a default of 0 instead of -1
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Monotonic decreasing stack; a bigger arrival resolves every smaller value waiting on top; unresolved indices default to 0
